The War of 1812 has ______ place in historical memory in Britain, partly because it is overshadowed by the much larger concurrent conflict against Napoleonic France and partly because it essentially maintained the geopolitical status quo for Britain: the country neither gained nor lost significant territory or position as a result of its participation in the war.

The 1904 city referendum has ______ place in local memory, partly because it is overshadowed by the far larger municipal reforms passed the following decade and partly because it essentially changed nothing about how the city was governed: the vote neither expanded nor restricted any existing office's authority.

The minor treaty of 1873 has ______ place in diplomatic history, partly because it is overshadowed by the much larger peace settlement signed only two years later and partly because it essentially preserved the prewar borders: neither side gained nor ceded any meaningful territory as a result.

The band's 1998 farewell tour has ______ place in music history, partly because it is overshadowed by the group's far more celebrated reunion a decade later and partly because it essentially changed nothing about the band's standing: their record sales and public profile remained about the same afterward.

The 1962 merger between the two small shipping companies has ______ place in business history, partly because it is overshadowed by the much larger industry consolidation that followed in the 1970s and partly because it essentially preserved each company's original routes: neither firm expanded nor lost any of its existing shipping lanes.

The senator's first term has ______ place in the state's political history, partly because it is overshadowed by the far more consequential term that followed and partly because it essentially maintained the legislative status quo: no major law was passed or repealed as a result of her time in office.

Historians argue that Karlsson's rejection of modern conveniences is ______ the house's reliance on skylights, thick stone walls, and hand-cranked ventilation shafts; these deliberately old-fashioned elements exemplify her design philosophy.

Critics argue that Rousseau's rejection of global trade is ______ the menu's exclusive reliance on produce grown within fifty kilometers of the restaurant; these locally sourced dishes exemplify his culinary philosophy.

Design historians argue that Brandt's rejection of decorative excess is ______ the typeface's stark, uniform strokes and complete absence of serifs; these austere features exemplify her design principles.

Planning historians argue that Duarte's rejection of car-centered design is ______ the neighborhood's narrow walkways and complete absence of parking lots; these deliberate choices exemplify his planning philosophy.

Craft historians argue that Fielding's rejection of industrial manufacturing is ______ the uneven glazes and irregular shapes of her finished pieces; these imperfect qualities exemplify her artistic values.

The following text is adapted from James Baldwin's 1956 novel Giovanni's Room.
The narrator is riding in a taxi down a street lined with food vendors and shoppers in Paris, France.
The multitude of Paris seems to be dressed in blue every day but Sunday, when, for the most part, they put on an unbelievably festive black.
Here they were now, in blue, disputing, every inch, our passage, with their wagons, handtrucks, their bursting baskets carried at an angle steeply self-confident on the back.
The following text is adapted from a novel.
The narrator is walking through a crowded market street at dusk.
Carts, crates, and the last stragglers of the evening crowd were disputing every inch of our path, each unwilling to yield the narrow lane before finishing whatever business had kept them there.
The narrator is trying to cross a flooded field after a storm.
Fallen branches and tangled undergrowth were disputing every step forward, each obstacle demanding to be climbed over or pushed aside before the next could even be seen.
The following text is adapted from a memoir.
The narrator is pushing through a crowded subway platform during rush hour.
Shoulders, bags, and elbows were disputing every foot of space, and by the time I reached the stairs my coat had been pulled nearly off one arm.
The following text is adapted from a short story.
The narrator is climbing a steep, overgrown trail at midday.
Roots, loose stones, and thick vines were disputing every stride uphill, so that what should have been an hour's walk stretched into most of the afternoon.
The narrator is wading through a crowded harbor market at midday.
Baskets, coiled ropes, and idle fishermen were disputing every step toward the dock, and I had to turn sideways more than once just to keep moving forward.
On painter William H. Johnson's return to the United States in 1938 after a decade in Europe, his style underwent an abrupt transformation.

Turning away from landscapes painted in an expressionist style—a style that often involves using fluid, distorted shapes and thick, textured brushstrokes to express the artist's subjective experience of reality—Johnson began painting portraits of Black Americans in a bold new way.
Evocative of African sculpture and American and Scandinavian folk art, these portraits feature flat, deliberately oversimplified figures in a vibrant but limited color palette.
On composer Ingrid Falk's return to Norway in 1952 after years abroad, her musical style underwent an abrupt transformation.
Turning away from the dense orchestral scores she had written throughout the 1940s, Falk began composing sparse chamber pieces built around long silences and single sustained notes.
Evocative of Norwegian folk fiddle traditions and the natural acoustics of fjord landscapes, these pieces feature minimal instrumentation and deliberately unresolved harmonies.
Upon novelist Teodor Basescu's release from a decade in political exile in 1987, his writing style underwent an abrupt transformation.
Turning away from the dense, allegorical prose he had published before his exile, Basescu began writing spare, plainly narrated short stories centered on ordinary daily routines.
Evocative of oral storytelling traditions and postwar minimalist fiction, these stories feature unadorned sentences and almost no figurative language.
After designer Naomi Achterberg relocated her studio from Paris to Lagos in 1975, her design style underwent an abrupt transformation.
Turning away from the closely tailored, monochrome silhouettes she had built her early reputation on, Achterberg began designing loose, brightly patterned garments cut from hand-dyed cotton.
Evocative of regional textile traditions and the bright light of the West African coast, these garments feature bold geometric prints and asymmetrical draping.
Following director Hassan Idrissi's return to Morocco in 1968 after film school abroad, his directing style underwent an abrupt transformation.
Turning away from the tightly scripted, dialogue-heavy films he had made as a student, Idrissi began directing loosely structured films built around long, unscripted takes of everyday street life.
Evocative of Italian neorealism and traditional Moroccan storytelling, these films feature nonprofessional actors and minimal editing.
After potter Junko Aoyama took over her family's workshop in 1990, her ceramic style underwent an abrupt transformation.
Turning away from the delicately painted porcelain her family had produced for generations, Aoyama began firing rough, unglazed stoneware left deliberately asymmetrical.
Evocative of centuries-old wabi-sabi aesthetics and the coastal clay of her hometown, these pieces feature visible cracks and uneven surfaces left exposed rather than smoothed away.

Scholarly accounts of the Chicano movement—a movement that advocated for the social, political, and cultural empowerment of Mexican Americans and reached its zenith in the 1960s and 1970s—tend to focus on the most militant, outspoken figures in the movement, making it seem uniformly radical.

Geographer Juan Herrera has shown, however, that if we shift our focus toward the way the movement manifested in comparatively low-profile neighborhood institutions and projects, we see participants espousing an array of political orientations and approaches to community activism.
Standard accounts of the guild movement in medieval textile towns tend to focus on the wealthiest master weavers, making the guilds seem uniformly prosperous.

Economic historian Ana Beltran has shown, however, that if we shift focus toward the far more numerous apprentice and journeyman weavers, we see participants facing a wide range of economic circumstances, from comfortable stability to persistent hardship.
Standard accounts of the abolitionist movement in a particular state tend to focus on its most prominent public speakers, making the movement seem uniformly confrontational in its tactics.

Historian Marcus DeWitt has shown, however, that if we shift focus toward the movement's local church-based and neighborhood organizing efforts, we see participants employing a wide range of strategies, from quiet fundraising to direct legal challenges.
Standard accounts of the early environmental movement tend to focus on its national lobbying organizations, making the movement seem uniformly focused on federal legislation.

Sociologist Priya Ramaswamy has shown, however, that if we shift focus toward small, community-led conservation projects of the same period, we see participants pursuing a wide range of goals, from local land trusts to neighborhood recycling programs.
Standard accounts of the early computer hobbyist movement tend to focus on a handful of well-known garage inventors, making the movement seem uniformly oriented toward commercial success.

Historian Wei Chen has shown, however, that if we shift focus toward the many small hobbyist clubs that met in libraries and community centers, we see participants pursuing a wide range of motivations, from pure curiosity to educational outreach.
Standard accounts of the settlement house movement tend to focus on its most famous founders, making the movement seem uniformly shaped by a single reform philosophy.

Historian Odalys Ferreira has shown, however, that if we shift focus toward the day-to-day staff who ran individual settlement houses, we see participants adopting a wide range of approaches, from strict vocational training to loosely structured community gatherings.

Since its completion in 2014, Bosco Verticale (Vertical Forest)—a pair of residential towers in Milan, Italy, covered by vegetation—has become a striking symbol of environmental sustainability in architecture.
Stefano Boeri intended his design, which features balconies that are home to hundreds of trees, to serve as a model for promoting urban biodiversity.

However, the concept has faced skepticism: critics note that although the trees used in Bosco Verticale were specifically cultivated for the project, it's too early to tell if they can thrive in this unusual setting.

Since its unveiling in 2019, the Solaris Canopy—a shading structure over a public plaza in Doha covered in photovoltaic-embedded fabric—has become a widely cited example of climate-adaptive architecture.
Designer Farah Haddad intended the fabric, which generates electricity while blocking direct sun, to serve as a model for hot-climate public spaces.

However, the concept has faced skepticism: critics note that although the fabric was specifically engineered for this installation, it's too early to tell if it can maintain its electrical output after years of exposure to blowing sand and extreme heat.
Since its completion in 2016, the Living Seawall—a stretch of artificial reef panels installed along a harbor in Sydney—has become a frequently cited example of urban marine restoration.
Engineer Devika Nair intended the textured panels, designed to mimic natural rock crevices, to serve as a model for restoring marine life along developed coastlines.

However, the concept has faced skepticism: critics note that although the panels were specifically molded for this harbor, it's too early to tell if the marine species they attract can establish a stable, self-sustaining population there.

Since its planting in 2018, the Whispering Grove—a stand of genetically modified drought-resistant oaks planted along a highway outside Phoenix—has become a frequently cited example of climate-resilient urban forestry.
Horticulturalist Marco Silva intended the trees, engineered to require minimal irrigation, to serve as a model for greening arid roadways.

However, the concept has faced skepticism: critics note that although the trees were specifically bred for this climate, it's too early to tell if their root systems can remain stable in the compacted soil found along most highway corridors.

Since its launch in 2021, the Tidal Lantern—a string of buoy-mounted turbines generating power from wave motion off the coast of Cornwall—has become a frequently cited example of small-scale marine energy.
Engineer Bryn Talbot intended the buoys, designed to flex with passing waves, to serve as a model for coastal renewable energy.

However, the concept has faced skepticism: critics note that although the buoys were specifically built for this stretch of coastline, it's too early to tell if their moving parts can withstand years of continuous storm exposure.
Since its opening in 2020, the Hollow Spire—a residential tower in Rotterdam built around a central column of vertical gardens—has become a frequently cited example of biophilic urban design.
Architect Lotte Bakker intended the column, irrigated by recycled greywater, to serve as a model for integrating greenery into dense housing.

However, the concept has faced skepticism: critics note that although the plants were specifically selected for this system, it's too early to tell if the greywater irrigation can reliably support them through the building's coldest winters.

Elizabeth Asiedu has identified a negative correlation between the share of developing countries' economies derived from natural-resource extraction and those countries' receipts of foreign investment.

This may appear counterintuitive—resource extraction requires initial investments (in extractive technology, for instance) at scales best met by multinational corporations—but Asiedu notes that natural-resource industries' boom-bust cycle can destabilize local currencies and increase developing countries' vulnerability to external shocks, creating levels of uncertainty to which foreign investors are typically averse.
Camille Duval has identified a negative correlation between the proportion of a city's downtown occupied by short-term vacation rentals and that city's long-term small-business survival rate.

This may appear counterintuitive—vacation rentals bring a steady stream of visitors who might be expected to support local shops—but Duval notes that the resulting spikes in rent, driven by property owners converting long-term leases into short-term rentals, price out the very small businesses that once served longtime residents, creating a less stable customer base overall.

Tomasz Wieczorek has identified a negative correlation between the share of a country's electricity generated from a newly built dam and that country's electricity price stability in the years immediately following construction.

This may appear counterintuitive—large dams are often expected to provide cheap, stable power—but Wieczorek notes that the debt taken on to finance construction, combined with unpredictable rainfall affecting output, can make electricity prices more volatile rather than less, at least until the debt is paid down.
Aisha Bello has identified a negative correlation between the number of self-checkout kiosks a grocery chain installs and that chain's overall customer satisfaction scores in the following year.

This may appear counterintuitive—self-checkout is often expected to reduce wait times and improve the shopping experience—but Bello notes that the resulting reduction in staffed checkout lanes can leave customers with complex purchases or technical problems with no easy source of help, lowering satisfaction overall.

Ravi Chandrasekaran has identified a negative correlation between the number of budget-priced streaming platforms a household subscribes to and that household's reported satisfaction with its overall entertainment options.

This may appear counterintuitive—more platforms are often expected to mean more content and greater choice—but Chandrasekaran notes that the resulting need to track multiple libraries, prices, and interfaces can create decision fatigue that leaves households feeling less satisfied rather than more.
Helena Kowalczyk has identified a negative correlation between the number of open-plan seating areas a company adds to its office and that company's employee-reported focus and productivity.

This may appear counterintuitive—open floor plans are often expected to boost collaboration and efficiency—but Kowalczyk notes that the resulting rise in ambient noise and visual distraction can make sustained concentration more difficult, lowering measured productivity rather than raising it.
Some astronomers searching for extraterrestrial life have proposed that atmospheric NH3 (ammonia) can serve as a biosignature gas—an indication that a planet harbors life.

Jingcheng Huang, Sara Seager, and colleagues evaluated this possibility, finding that on rocky planets, atmospheric NH3 likely couldn't reach detectably high levels in the absence of biological activity.

But the team also found that on so-called mini-Neptunes—gas planets smaller than Neptune but with atmospheres similar to Neptune's—atmospheric pressure and temperature can be high enough to produce atmospheric NH3.
Some astrobiologists have proposed that atmospheric phosphine can serve as a biosignature gas—an indication that a planet harbors life.

Elena Marchetti and colleagues evaluated this possibility, finding that on small rocky planets, atmospheric phosphine likely couldn't reach detectably high levels in the absence of biological activity.
But the team also found that on gas giants with deep, high-pressure atmospheres, phosphine can form abiotically under extreme temperature and pressure alone.
Some astrobiologists have proposed that atmospheric methyl chloride can serve as a biosignature gas.

Dara Osei and colleagues evaluated this possibility, finding that on small rocky planets orbiting quiet stars, atmospheric methyl chloride likely couldn't reach detectably high levels in the absence of biological activity.
But the team also found that on rocky planets orbiting highly active, flaring stars, methyl chloride can form abiotically through intense stellar radiation striking the atmosphere.
Some astrobiologists have proposed that atmospheric dimethyl sulfide can serve as a biosignature gas.

Jorge Villalobos and colleagues evaluated this possibility, finding that on planets with thin, oxygen-poor atmospheres, atmospheric dimethyl sulfide likely couldn't reach detectably high levels in the absence of biological activity.
But the team also found that on planets with thick, sulfur-rich volcanic atmospheres, dimethyl sulfide can form abiotically through ongoing volcanic outgassing alone.
Some astrobiologists have proposed that atmospheric nitrous oxide can serve as a biosignature gas.

Priya Deshmukh and colleagues evaluated this possibility, finding that on temperate rocky planets, atmospheric nitrous oxide likely couldn't reach detectably high levels in the absence of biological activity.
But the team also found that on rocky planets subjected to frequent large asteroid impacts, nitrous oxide can form abiotically through the intense heat and chemical shock of repeated collisions.
Some astrobiologists have proposed that atmospheric ethane can serve as a biosignature gas.

Soren Lindqvist and colleagues evaluated this possibility, finding that on rocky planets with liquid-water oceans, atmospheric ethane likely couldn't reach detectably high levels in the absence of biological activity.
But the team also found that on icy moons with subsurface methane lakes, ethane can form abiotically through ultraviolet radiation breaking down methane in the upper atmosphere.
Under normal atmospheric pressure at Earth's surface, water molecules form a tetrahedral network stabilized by hydrogen bonds between adjacent molecules.

Extreme high pressure, such as can be found in deep ocean waters, destabilizes these bonds and compresses water's structure, allowing water molecules within organisms to permeate proteins and impede crucial biological functions; yet deep-sea organisms known as piezophiles have adapted to extreme pressure.

Studies have found a positive correlation between the depths that various piezophiles inhabit and concentrations of a compound called trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) in their muscle tissues, which has led a team of researchers to hypothesize that TMAO reduces water's compressibility.
Under normal atmospheric pressure, cell membranes maintain a flexible, semi-fluid lipid structure.
Extreme cold, such as found in polar waters, rigidifies this structure and can impair nutrient transport across the membrane; yet cold-adapted fish have evolved to survive these temperatures.

Studies have found a positive correlation between the depths at which various cold-adapted fish live and concentrations of unsaturated fatty acids in their cell membranes, leading a team of researchers to hypothesize that these fatty acids reduce the membrane's tendency to stiffen in the cold.
Under normal soil conditions, plant root cell walls maintain a semi-rigid structure that allows for steady water uptake.
Extreme salinity, such as found in coastal floodplains, destabilizes this structure and can impair water absorption; yet certain salt-tolerant grasses have adapted to these conditions.

Studies have found a positive correlation between the salinity levels grasses tolerate and concentrations of a compound called glycine betaine in their root cells, leading a team of researchers to hypothesize that glycine betaine reduces the cell wall's vulnerability to salt-induced damage.
Under normal temperatures, insect cuticle maintains a hardened, protective structure.
Extreme heat, such as found during heat waves, softens this structure and can leave insects vulnerable to water loss; yet certain desert beetles have adapted to survive such heat.

Studies have found a positive correlation between the temperatures desert beetles can withstand and concentrations of a wax-like compound in their cuticle, leading a team of researchers to hypothesize that this compound reduces the cuticle's tendency to soften in extreme heat.
Under normal light levels, the pigment-protein complexes in certain algae maintain a stable folded structure.

Extreme sunlight, such as found near the ocean's surface at midday, destabilizes these complexes and can impair photosynthesis; yet some surface-dwelling algae have adapted to withstand intense light.

Studies have found a positive correlation between the light intensities algae can tolerate and concentrations of a carotenoid pigment within their cells, leading a team of researchers to hypothesize that this carotenoid reduces the complexes' vulnerability to light-induced damage.
Under normal humidity, spider silk maintains a tightly coiled molecular structure that gives it its strength.
Extreme dryness, such as found in arid habitats, disrupts this structure and can make the silk brittle; yet certain desert spiders produce silk that withstands such conditions.

Studies have found a positive correlation between the dryness levels a spider's habitat reaches and concentrations of a particular protein in its silk, leading a team of researchers to hypothesize that this protein reduces the silk's tendency to become brittle in dry conditions.

Consider the mechanics of the pinhole camera: light passes through a small hole, resulting in a focused projected image.

A ray diagram reveals how this ______ the hole's small size restricts light to a single ray, all light passing through the hole can only arrive at a single destination, eliminating diffraction and ensuring a clear image.
Consider the mechanics of a simple lever: a small force applied far from the pivot lifts a much larger weight placed close to it.

A force diagram reveals how this ______ the pivot's position determines how far each end must travel, all the force applied at the long end is multiplied at the short end, producing greater lifting power.
Consider the mechanics of a prism: white light entering one face exits the other split into a visible band of colors.
A ray diagram reveals how this ______ each wavelength of light bends by a slightly different amount, all the colors that entered together spread apart as they exit, producing a visible spectrum.
Consider the mechanics of a suspension bridge: the roadway hangs from cables anchored at towers on either end.

Consider the mechanics of a refrigerator: a warm kitchen stays separate from a cold interior compartment.

Consider the mechanics of a telescope: distant, dim objects appear brighter and larger than they do to the naked eye.

An optical diagram reveals how this ______ a large primary lens or mirror gathers far more light than the human eye can on its own, all the collected light is focused into a single, magnified image, revealing detail invisible without the instrument.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Earthquakes start at a point called a "focus" and spread out from there as seismic waves.
- The two types of seismic waves that travel beneath Earth's surface are primary waves (P waves) and secondary waves (S waves).
- P waves travel more quickly beneath Earth's surface than do S waves.
- P waves compress and expand the ground, causing it to move backward and forward.
- S waves cause the ground to move from side to side.
- Hurricanes and typhoons are both large rotating storm systems that form over warm ocean water.
- Hurricanes form over the Atlantic and northeastern Pacific; typhoons form over the northwestern Pacific.
- Hurricanes are categorized using the Saffir-Simpson scale; typhoons are categorized using a different regional scale.
- Both storm types draw energy from warm ocean surface temperatures.
- Both storm types can produce sustained winds exceeding 150 miles per hour.
- Cellos and double basses are both string instruments played with a bow.
- Cellos are tuned in fifths; double basses are tuned in fourths.
- Cellos are typically played while seated with the instrument between the knees; double basses are typically played standing or on a stool.
- Both instruments have four main strings in their standard configuration.
- Both instruments provide the bass foundation in an orchestral string section.
- Octopuses and cuttlefish are both cephalopods capable of rapidly changing the color and texture of their skin.
- Octopuses have eight arms; cuttlefish have eight arms plus two longer feeding tentacles.
- Octopuses generally lack an internal shell; cuttlefish have an internal structure called a cuttlebone.
- Both animals use specialized skin cells called chromatophores to change color almost instantly.
- Octopuses are typically solitary, while cuttlefish are sometimes found in small groups.
- Maple syrup and agave syrup are both natural liquid sweeteners derived from plants.
- Maple syrup is made by boiling down the sap of maple trees; agave syrup is made by processing the sap of the agave plant.
- Maple syrup has a moderate glycemic index; agave syrup has a lower glycemic index.
- Both sweeteners can be substituted for refined sugar in most baking recipes.
- Maple syrup is primarily produced in North America; agave syrup is primarily produced in Mexico.
- Solar panels and wind turbines are both renewable energy technologies that generate electricity without burning fossil fuels.
- Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity; wind turbines convert the kinetic energy of moving air.
- Solar panels produce more consistently during daylight hours; wind turbines can generate power at any time of day.
- Both technologies require little water to operate compared with traditional power plants.
- Solar panel installations are often placed on rooftops; wind turbines are typically installed in open, elevated areas.
- The US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) keeps a list of all at-risk species.
- Species on the list are classified as either endangered or threatened.
- A species that is in danger of extinction throughout most or all of its range is classified as endangered.
- A species that is likely to soon become endangered is classified as threatened.
- The California red-legged frog (Rana draytonii) is likely to soon become endangered, according to the FWS.
- The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) maintains a Red List of species conservation status.
- Species are classified in several categories, including "Vulnerable" and "Endangered."
- A species facing a high risk of extinction in the wild is classified as Vulnerable.
- A species facing a very high risk of extinction in the wild is classified as Endangered.
- The Sumatran orangutan faces an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild, according to the IUCN.
- A national weather service classifies winter storm warnings into two levels: "Advisory" and "Warning."
- An Advisory is issued when snowfall is expected to cause significant inconvenience but not a serious hazard.
- A Warning is issued when snowfall is expected to create a serious hazard to life and property.
- Meteorologists forecast that the approaching storm will drop enough snow to create a serious hazard to life and property in the region.
